title: Your heartbeat
hookLine: it has been beating since before you could ask it to, and it has never once waited for permission

cards: Put two fingers on the inside of your wrist, just below the thumb. Press lightly. Wait.
There it is: a small knock, then another, then another. It was going on while you slept, while you argued, while you laughed at something dumb.
You never asked it to start this morning, and you can't make it stop by deciding to. Breath, yesterday, you could at least hold for a moment. This one doesn't take requests.
It just keeps going, from somewhere below the part of you that makes plans.

teach.b: First, the plain fact of it. You did not build this. Nobody does.

It was beating before you had a name, and every beat since has arrived without a single decision from you. Mostly that's a relief: if you had to remember each beat, you'd never get anything else done.
Second, a heart that stays awake.

teach.h: I SLEEP, BUT MY HEART WAKETH.
teach.b: In the Song of Songs, a book of love poems in the Hebrew Bible, a lover says, in the King James words: "I sleep, but my heart waketh: it is the voice of my beloved that knocketh."
The body is asleep; the heart is not, and the next sound in the poem is a knock at the door.

Readers have taken the line as love between two people, and some Jewish and Christian readers have also heard in it a soul that stays awake to God. Either way, it's the knock at your wrist. Third, the heart as a source.

teach.h: KEEP THY HEART: THE ISSUES OF LIFE.
teach.b: Proverbs says: "Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life." In Proverbs the heart is more than a muscle. It stands for the inner self, where a person thinks and chooses.
Life flows out from it, so the verse asks that it be guarded. Fourth, why it matters on an ordinary afternoon. Awe often goes looking for something large: a canyon, a storm, a sky full of stars.

teach.h: A WONDER YOU CAN'T LEAVE AT HOME.
teach.b: The pulse is tiny and always there, a wonder you can carry anywhere.
You can't leave it at home.

how: Some meditation teachers in Buddhist and secular settings invite students to rest attention on the pulse or the chest, and some Jewish and Christian readers pray with the Song of Songs as a love poem between the soul and God.

o: a small knock that keeps going without your permission
a feeling of love the Song says should be guarded
the rhythm a drum keeps in worship and song

games.q: you're the lover in the Song of Songs, asleep at night. what is your heart doing?
o: sleeping, like the rest of you.
waking, and hearing the beloved knock.
games.why: "I sleep, but my heart waketh: it is the voice of my beloved that knocketh." the body rests; the heart keeps listening.

practice: Find your pulse again, at the wrist or the side of your neck, or rest a hand flat on your chest, and don't count, because counting turns it into a test.
Let each beat arrive, and notice it arrived without you; if your mind wanders, the beat will still be there when you come back.
If you pray, rest the Song's words on the rhythm, I sleep, but my heart waketh; if you don't, keep company with the knock under your fingers.

wordCard.voice: Your heartbeat. The small knock under your fingers that never waits for permission, and keeps going even while you sleep. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: heart, the word in Proverbs 4:23. in Proverbs the heart is also where a person thinks and chooses.

carryVoice: Your line: it keeps beating. Even now, under everything, it's keeping time. Till tomorrow, then.
